title: Kind Clicks
tagline: Children sort online messages into kind clicks and stop-and-tell moments, turn unkind words into kind ones, and practice asking a trusted grown-up for help.
groupSize: Whole class, then pairs; any class size
overview: Many young children already send hearts, stickers, and messages in games, class apps, and video chats with family. Words on a screen still land on a real person. In this lesson children watch a paper heart get crumpled by unkind words, sort messages into **Kind Click** (a heart made with their hands) and **Stop and Tell** (a stop hand), rewrite unkind messages into kind ones, and rehearse the exact words to use with a trusted grown-up. Messages that celebrate differences are part of the kind set, so children also practice welcoming friends who like different things.
objectives: Students will sort online messages into kind and unkind or unsafe, and explain one choice.
Students will change an unkind message into a kind one, out loud or in writing.
Students will practice telling a trusted grown-up, using the sentence "I saw something online that made me feel ___. Can you help?"
Students will give a kind response to a friend who likes something different from them.

print: Handout A: Kind Click or Stop and Tell? sort strips (1 teacher set, cut apart)
Handout B: Fix-It Cards (1 set per 2–3 pairs, cut apart)
Handout C: My Kind Click (1 per student)
A large paper heart cut from construction paper; two signs: KIND CLICK (heart hands) and STOP AND TELL (stop hand); crayons
digital: Optional: the class's own approved messaging, comment, or learning app, shown by the teacher on the projector
Optional: a slide with a mock chat window so the sort items look like real messages

prep: Cut out a large paper heart and practice the crumple-and-smooth demonstration.
Cut apart the 12 strips from Handout A and the 8 Fix-It Cards from Handout B.
Post the two signs on opposite sides of the room.
Decide who children should name as trusted grown-ups at school (you, the counselor, the principal) so you can say their names.

steps.title: The wrinkled heart
steps.body: Hold up the paper heart and name it after a pretend child, "Remy." Read three unkind online messages sent to Remy ("Your drawing is ugly." "Nobody wants to play with you." "Everyone laugh at Remy's video."). Crumple the heart a little with each one. Then say "Sorry, Remy" and try to smooth it. Ask: **"Is the heart the same as before?"** Say: "Words on a screen still go to a real person. Today we practice kind clicks."
steps.note: Name Remy as pretend so no child in class feels singled out. Keep the heart posted for the rest of the week.

steps.title: Two signals
steps.body: Teach the two hand signals. **KIND CLICK**: make a heart with your hands. **STOP AND TELL**: hold up a flat hand like a stop sign, then point to a trusted grown-up. Explain: "STOP AND TELL means: don't send a mean message back, don't keep it a secret, tell a grown-up." Model one strip from Handout A out loud: "'Can I help you with that level?' That's helpful and kind. Heart hands!"
steps.note: Stress the "don't send a mean one back" part. Young children often think fighting back is fair.

steps.title: Sort the messages
steps.body: Read each strip in a normal voice (not a mean voice). Children show heart hands or the stop hand. Hand the strip to a child who walks it to the matching sign. Ask one child per strip: **"How would that message make someone feel?"** For strips about liking different things, ask: "Is it OK that your friend likes something different? What could you say?"
steps.note: The strip about sharing a funny photo of a friend without asking often surprises children. It may feel fun, but it isn't kind if the friend didn't say yes.

steps.title: Fix-it and tell-a-grown-up
steps.body: Give each pair a Fix-It Card. Partners read (or you read) the unkind message and together say a kind message instead. Share three or four aloud. Then role-play telling: one partner is the child, one is the trusted grown-up. The child says: **"I saw something online that made me feel ___. Can you help?"** The grown-up answers: "Thank you for telling me. Let's look at it together." Switch roles.
steps.note: The Fix-It Card backs give a sample kind message. Accept any kind version the pair invents; their own words stick better.

steps.title: My Kind Click
steps.body: Children complete Handout C: draw or write a kind message for a friend, draw a friend who likes something different and a kind thing to say to them, draw their trusted grown-up, and finish "When I see something mean online, I will…" Invite a few children to read their kind message to the wrinkled heart.
steps.note: Collect Handout C as evidence. The key sentence is the "I will" line: look for "stop and tell a grown-up."

unplugged: The lesson is fully unplugged: the paper heart, printed strips, hand signals, and role-play need no devices. You can write the sort messages in speech bubbles on the board to make them look like a chat.
digital: Project the messaging or comment feature of an app your class already uses (or a mock chat on a slide) and type two or three sort messages into it so children see how they look on a screen. As a class, compose one kind comment together on a classmate's shared work, with the classmate's permission, and let the class decide if it passes the kind-click test before you post. Children do not need their own accounts; you type.
whyTech: Kindness and help-seeking are best practiced face to face, so this lesson is unplugged at its core. Seeing and composing a real message on the projector adds a bridge: children connect the kind words they practiced to the screen where they'll use them.

adaptations.label: Kindergarten
adaptations.text: Use 8 strips and focus on the two signals; skip writing on Handout C and let children dictate their kind message.

adaptations.label: Grade 2
adaptations.text: Pairs write their own Fix-It Card (an unkind message on the front, a kind fix on the back) and trade with another pair.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Hand signals carry the meaning. Offer the kind-message sentence frames in both languages and let children say the fix in either one.

adaptations.label: Social-emotional support
adaptations.text: Let the school counselor co-teach the tell-a-grown-up role-play, and name the counselor as a trusted grown-up.

lookFors: Children choose STOP AND TELL for messages that are mean, share others' photos without asking, or ask for passwords, and explain how the message would make someone feel.
Pairs turn unkind messages into kind ones in their own words.
Children use the full tell-a-grown-up sentence in the role-play and on Handout C.
Children give kind responses to classmates who like different games, foods, or activities.
reflection: How would you feel if you got that message? How can we make someone's heart feel better?
How well do I work with others when we learn together? (Student ELE guiding question)
Who will you tell if you see something mean online?
transfer: Send home the tell-a-grown-up sentence so families can practice it, and invite families to write one kind message together to a relative, on paper or on screen. Next lesson, use the kind-click signals during classroom partner work, not only online.

connections.title: Digital Citizenship Breakouts (K–8)
connections.note: A teacher-led digital breakout follow-up on digital citizenship.

handouts.title: Kind Click or Stop and Tell?
handouts.instructions: Teacher: read each message aloud. Children show heart hands or a stop hand. Tape it under the sign.

items.why: It makes a friend feel proud.

items.text: "Can I help you with that level?"
"You like a different game than me. Cool! Show me yours."
items.why: It welcomes a friend who likes something different.
It hurts feelings. Don't answer back; tell a grown-up.
Leaving someone out on purpose hurts.
It gets others to be unkind too.

items.text: "Send me your password or you're not my friend."
items.why: Unkind and unsafe. Passwords stay private.

items.text: "Let's share the silly photo of Theo sleeping. Don't tell him!"
items.why: Theo didn't say yes. Sharing it could hurt him.

items.text: "Your way of doing it is weird. Do it my way."
items.why: Different ways are OK. This message makes someone feel bad.

handouts.title: Fix-It Cards
handouts.instructions: Read the unkind message. With your partner, say a KIND message instead. The back shows one idea.

cards.label: Fix it
cards.back: Try: "I like the colors you used!"

cards.label: Fix it
cards.back: Try: "Do you want to play with us?"

cards.label: Fix it
cards.back: Try: "I haven't played that. How does it work?"

cards.label: Fix it
cards.front: "You lost. You're so bad at this."
cards.back: Try: "Good game! Want to play again?"

cards.label: Fix it
cards.back: Try: "My favorite part was the ending!"

cards.label: Fix it
cards.front: "Why do you eat that weird food?"
cards.back: Try: "What does it taste like? Can you tell me about it?"

cards.label: Fix it
cards.back: Try: "Thanks for making a video. I liked the funny part."

cards.label: Fix it
cards.front: "Go away, this chat is only for us."

handouts.title: My Kind Click
handouts.instructions: Draw or write. Your teacher can help with words.

sections.prompt: Draw or write a KIND message I could send to a friend.
Draw a friend who likes something different from me. What kind thing could I say?
Draw my trusted grown-up. Write their name.
When I see something mean online, I will ___.
